query: For high-entropy alloys intended for extreme environments, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve elevated-temperature mechanical properties? State the intervention without limiting its class, the proposed mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the temperature and application boundaries under which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment whose outcome would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing serrated grain boundary morphology via a controlled slow cooling step in the post-solution heat treatment will improve the elevated-temperature mechanical performance of precipitation‐strengthened high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy processed via conventional rapid cooling that exhibits predominantly straight grain boundaries and a precipitation-strengthened microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply a slower cooling rate during the post-solution heat treatment to allow coarsening of coherent precipitates that interact with mobile grain boundaries and induce a serrated (undulated) grain boundary morphology.
generation.conditions: Testing at elevated temperatures around 650°C under conditions relevant to extreme environment applications (e.g., nuclear reactors or aerospace components).
generation.structural_mediator: Serrated grain boundaries formed via precipitate coarsening at the grain and phase boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The undulated (serrated) grain boundaries reduce local strain concentrations and impede intergranular crack propagation, thereby enhancing both creep resistance and tensile ductility at elevated temperatures by redistributing stress more uniformly along the grain boundaries.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the conventional (straight) grain boundary microstructure, the treated alloy is expected to exhibit a significant increase in tensile ductility (notably a 3–4× improvement in fracture strain) and an order-of-magnitude improvement in creep rupture life (potentially up to 400× longer) at 650°C.
generation.baseline: HEAs subjected to standard rapid-cooling protocols that yield straight grain boundaries with known hot ductility loss and lower creep resistance at 650°C.
generation.boundary: This improvement is predicted to hold for precipitation‐strengthened HEAs in the 600–700°C range; its applicability to other HEA families or at temperatures significantly higher than 700°C is uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the mechanical improvements may vary depending on the specific alloy composition and processing parameters; it is also uncertain whether all HEA systems with precipitation strengthening will respond similarly to the induced serrated grain boundary morphology.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical precipitation-strengthened HEA specimens. One set undergoes a modified slow cooling post-solution heat treatment to induce serrated grain boundaries, while the control set is subjected to a standard rapid-cooling process producing straight grain boundaries. Conduct elevated-temperature tensile and creep tests at 650°C.
measurements: Grain boundary morphology characterization (via SEM or TEM) to verify serration
Tensile fracture strain and tensile strength at 650°C
Creep rupture life and minimum creep strain rate at 650°C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If specimens receiving the slow cooling treatment do not exhibit a statistically significant increase (e.g., >3× improvement in ductility and >10× improvement in creep rupture life) over the control, or if the expected serrated grain boundary morphology is not observed, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: ABSTRACTIn this study, tensile and creep deformation of a high-entropy alloy processed by selective laser melting (SLM) has been investigated; hot ductility drop was identified at first, and the loss of ductility at elevated temperature was associated with intergranular fracture. By modifying the grain boundary morphology from straight to serration, the hot ductility drop issue has been resolved successfully. The serrated grain boundary could be achieved by reducing the cooling rate of solution heat treatment, which allowed the coarsening of L12 structured γ′ precipitates to interfere with mobile grain boundaries, resulting in undulation of the grain boundary morphology. Tensile and creep tests at 650°C were conducted, and serrated grain boundary could render a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life by a factor of 3.5 and 400, respectively. Detailed microstructure analysis has indicated that serrated grain boundary could distribute strains more evenly than that of straight morphology. However, thermo-mechanical process is not applicable as a post processing step for SLM, where components are usually built closely to the final dimension. Another possible approach to resolve the hot ductility loss is to introduce serrated grain boundary (SEGB) [], it usually involves a post heat treatment step to induce interactions between mobile grain boundaries and second phases, including carbides [], δ phase [], or γ′ phase []. SEGB has been reported to impede intergranular crack propagation [,,], improve the tensile properties of Ni-based superalloys fabricated by SLM [], and also the ductility of Ni46.23Co23Cr10Fe5Al8.5Ti4W2Mo1C0.15B0.1Zr0.02 fabricated by arc melting []. In this study, we have unprecedentedly utilized SEGB on an HEA fabricated by SLM. This work is the first to investigate the underlying mechanism of hot ductility drop of a HEA fabricated by SLM and study the effect of SEGB on its high temperature tensile and creep properties.

Observations suggest that serrated grain boundary could serve as a crack deflector and retard connection of microcracks. Simulation results demonstrated that severely localized strains at triple junctions, by contrast strains were more homogeneous distributed along serrated grain boundaries.
